# 🧠 Rust's Memory Safety Features

Rust ensures memory safety through compile-time checks and a unique set of language features that eliminate common bugs like null pointers, use-after-free, and data races — all without needing a garbage collector.

---

## 1. 🏷 Ownership

- Every value has a single owner.
- When the owner goes out of scope, the value is automatically dropped (deallocated).
- Prevents double free and dangling pointers.

```rust
let s = String::from("hello");
let t = s; // s is moved, no longer valid

2. 🔄 Borrowing

Allows references to data without transferring ownership.

You can have:

One mutable reference or

Any number of immutable references

Enforced at compile time to avoid data races.

rust
Copy
Edit
fn print_length(s: &String) {
    println!("{}", s.len());
}

3. ⏳ Lifetimes

Lifetimes specify how long references are valid.

Ensure that references don’t outlive the data they point to.

Prevents dangling references.

rust
Copy
Edit
fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() { x } else { y }
}

4. 🚫 No Null or Undefined Values

Rust does not have null; uses Option<T> instead.

Forces developers to handle the "none" case explicitly.

rust
Copy
Edit
let name: Option<String> = Some(String::from("Alice"));

5. 🧵 Thread Safety

Rust's type system ensures safe data access across threads.

Types like Arc and Mutex are used to share data safely.

rust
Copy
Edit
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
let data = Arc::new(Mutex::new(5));

✅ Summary

Rust’s memory safety is guaranteed by its ownership model, borrowing rules, and lifetime tracking, all enforced at compile time. This eliminates many classes of memory bugs without a garbage collector.
